{{Short description|Infinite series summable to 1}}
[[File:Eye of Horus square.svg|thumb|First six summands drawn as portions of a square.]]
[[File:Geometric Segment.svg|thumb|The geometric series on the real line.]]

In [[mathematics]], the [[infinite series]] {{nowrap|'''{{sfrac|1|2}} + {{sfrac|1|4}} + {{sfrac|1|8}} + {{sfrac|1|16}} + ···'''}} is an elementary example of a [[geometric series]] that [[absolute convergence|converges absolutely]]. The sum of the series is 1.
In [[Capital-sigma notation|summation notation]], this may be expressed as
:<math>\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\frac{1}{16}+\cdots = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left({\frac 12}\right)^n = 1. </math>

The series is related to philosophical questions considered in antiquity, particularly to [[Zeno's paradoxes]].

==Proof==
 
As with any [[Series (mathematics)|infinite series]], the sum
:<math>\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\frac{1}{16}+\cdots</math>
is defined to mean the [[Limit of a sequence|limit]] of the [[partial sum]] of the first {{mvar|n}} terms 
:<math>s_n=\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\frac{1}{16}+\cdots+\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}+\frac{1}{2^n}</math>
as {{mvar|n}} approaches infinity, if it exists.
By various arguments,{{efn|For example: multiplying {{mvar|s<sub>n</sub>}} by 2 yields <math>2s_n = \frac22+\frac24+\frac28+\frac{2}{16}+\cdots+\frac{2}{2^n} = 1+\left[\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\cdots+\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right] = 1+\left[s_n-\frac{1}{2^{n}}\right].</math> Subtracting {{mvar|s<sub>n</sub>}} from both sides, one concludes <math>s_n = 1-\frac{1}{2^{n}}.</math>  Other arguments might proceed by [[mathematical induction]], or by adding <math>\frac{1}{2^n}</math> to both sides of <math>s_n=\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\frac{1}{16}+\cdots+\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}+\frac{1}{2^n}</math> and manipulating to show that the right side of the result is equal to 1.{{cn|date=November 2020}}}}<ref>Abramowitz, M.; Stegun, I. A., eds. (1972). ''[[Handbook of Mathematical Functions with Formulas, Graphs, and Mathematical Tables]]'' (9th printing). New York: Dover. p. 10.</ref> one can show that each finite sum is equal to
:<math>s_n = 1-\frac{1}{2^{n}},</math>
and as {{mvar|n}} approaches infinity, the term <math>\frac{1}{2^{n}}</math> approaches 0 and so {{mvar|s<sub>n</sub>}} approaches 1.

==History==
===Zeno's paradox===
This series was used as a representation of two of [[Zeno's paradoxes]].<ref name="Description of Zeno's paradoxe...">Field, Paul and Weisstein, Eric W. "Zeno's Paradoxes." From MathWorld--A Wolfram Web Resource. https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ZenosParadoxes.html</ref>  For example, in the [[Achilles and the Tortoise|paradox of Achilles and the Tortoise]], the warrior Achilles was to race against a tortoise. The track is 100 meters long. Achilles could run at 10&nbsp;m/s, while the tortoise only 5. The tortoise, with a 10-meter advantage, Zeno argued, would win. Achilles would have to move 10 meters to catch up to the tortoise, but the tortoise would already have moved another five meters by then. Achilles would then have to move 5 meters, where the tortoise would move 2.5 meters, and so on. Zeno argued that the tortoise would always remain ahead of Achilles. Similarly, Zeno's [[dichotomy paradox]] arises from the supposition that to move a certain distance, one would have to move half of it, then half of the remaining distance, and so on, therefore having infinitely many time intervals.<ref name="Description of Zeno's paradoxe...">Field, Paul and Weisstein, Eric W. "Zeno's Paradoxes." From MathWorld--A Wolfram Web Resource. https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ZenosParadoxes.html</ref> 

In both cases, each time interval is a term of this [[infinite geometric series]], and so even in the limit of infinite terms it would sum to a finite total time. This is sometimes considered to resolve Zeno's paradoxes.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |year=2010 |title=Zeno's Paradoxes: 5. Zeno's Influence on Philosophy |encyclopedia=[[Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]] |url=http://plato.stanford.edu/entries/paradox-zeno/#ZenInf |access-date=2011-03-07 |last=Huggett |first=Nick |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220301174333/https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/paradox-zeno/#ZenInf |archive-date=2022-03-01 |url-status=live}}</ref> However, insofar as Zeno was concerned with the problems of division of a continuum into an [[actual infinity]] of sub-parts, rather than the problem of their sum, it may not address the philosophical heart of Zeno's argument.<ref name="Papa-G">{{cite journal |last=Papa-Grimaldi |first=Alba |year=1996 |title=Why Mathematical Solutions of Zeno's Paradoxes Miss the Point: Zeno's One and Many Relation and Parmenides' Prohibition |url=http://philsci-archive.pitt.edu/2304/1/zeno_maths_review_metaphysics_alba_papa_grimaldi.pdf |url-status=live |journal=The Review of Metaphysics |volume=50 |pages=299–314 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120609113959/http://philsci-archive.pitt.edu/2304/1/zeno_maths_review_metaphysics_alba_papa_grimaldi.pdf |archive-date=2012-06-09 |access-date=2012-03-06}}</ref>

===The Eye of Horus===
The parts of the [[Eye of Horus#In arithmetic|Eye of Horus]] were once thought to represent the first six summands of the series.<ref>{{cite book | title=Professor Stewart's Hoard of Mathematical Treasures | last=Stewart | first=Ian | publisher=Profile Books | isbn=978-1-84668-292-6 | year= 2009 | pages=76–80 }}</ref>

===In ''Zhuangzi'' ===
A version of the series appears in the ancient [[Taoism|Taoist]] book ''[[Zhuangzi (book)|Zhuangzi]]''. The miscellaneous chapters "All Under Heaven" include the following sentence: "Take a [[Chi (length)|chi]] long stick and remove half every day, in a myriad ages it will not be exhausted."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Fraser |first1=Chris |title=School of Names > Miscellaneous Paradoxes (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy) |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/school-names/paradoxes.html |website=plato.stanford.edu |access-date=24 July 2025 |language=en}}</ref>
